In 1921, eighty-two vessels loaded at the port of Vancouver with 127,000 tons of freight, and pasesd through the Panama canal to the Atlantic. In 1923, 200 vessels loaded 677,000 tons of freight and passed through the Panama canal to the Atlantic.
The development has been rapid; but I think it has really only started, because we in western Canada, and, I believe, the people in eastern Canada, and the people in the Old Country, have begun to realize the advantage of the Panama canal and the possibilities of the extension of business in the Pacific and the Orient. The primary stimulus to this movement can, I think, be set down to the reduction in freight rates, resulting in a partial elimination of the mountain scale. In 1922 the government of the province of British Columbia presented argument to the Board of Railway Commissioners and succeeded in getting some relief under a general order No. 366, issued on the 30th June, 1922, by the board. I might say that there has always been a division of freight rates into class and commodity rates, the first being based1 on mileage and considered as standard, and second, commodity rates which are not based upon mileage, but are made by all railways as when they consider necessary in order to move traffic. About 15 per cent of the total traffic to and from British Columbia moves on class rates, the balance on commodity rates. Prior to the date of the judgment
the British Columbia class rates scale, generally speaking, was based on 14 times the prairie scale, which, worked1 out, meant that the mountain scale was about 33 per cent greater than the prairie scale. By this judgment the differential was cut in two and the mountain scale is now -about 165 per cent greater than the prairie.
At the time of this judgment the amount of grain moving to Vancouver for export was comparatively small. Grain and grain products for domestic consumption moved upon commodity rates. The board ordered that the commodity rate for wheat and wheat products for domestic consumption should be reduced by the same percentage as the class rate; but as the rate on grain and grain products for export was scarcely referred to in the argument before the board, the board did not take action in regard to it. However, on the issuance of the order the railways themselves made a reduction of 20 per cent in the export rates on grain and grain products. That was in the spring of 1922, and it will be noted that the exports, which were 700,000 bushels the year before, jumped to 7,000,000 bushels.
The British Columbia government, although receiving some concession at the hands of the Railway Commission, appealed from that judgment to the executive council. A hearing was had during the summer months, and I propose now to quote from the reference of the executive council to the railway board of October 2nd of that year the section relating to grain and other rates. It is as follows:
And it appearing that the question as to the rates on grain from points in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to Vancouver and other British Columbia coast points for export was not the subject of argument before the board and therefore not specifically dealt with in its said judgment;
And it appearing further that on the hearing of the said appeal the petitioners asked for reductions in the said rates on grain;
The committee therefore recommends that the subject of the said export grain rates from points in the said provinces to Vancouver and other British Columbia coast points be referred to the said board for immediate consideration and such effective action as it may deem necessary.
It will be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the reference was made at the beginning of October last year, it being the desire of the government that if further reductions could be made in the grain rates the matter should be dealt with early by the Board of Railway Commissioners in the hope of securing further relief. The Board of Railway Commissioners on the 10th October, 1923, issued the following order, No. 384:
Whereas by order in council P.C. No. 2007, dated the 2nd day of October, 1923, the Governor in Council referred the subject of the said export grain rates from

The Address-Mr. King (Kootenay)
points in the said provinces to Vancouver and other British Columbia coast points, to the board for immediate determination and such effective action as the board may deem necessary;
After fully considering the matter and applying the principles set forth in the judgment of the board, dated October 10th, 1923, and for the reasons therein contained-
The board orders that the current rates on grain and grain products to Pacific coast ports for export be reduced uniformly ten per cent; and that all the railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of the board file tariffs, effective not later than October 22nd, 1923, showing such reduction; also that all milling, malting, storage, cleaning or bagging in transit privileges on grain now contained in the tariffs be unaffected bv this order.
# Mr. CLARK: When the Railway Commission was directed to review these rates, did counsel appear on behalf of the province of British Columba?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, I think not. Counsel for British Columbia appeared before the Railway Commission in the spring of 1922, and they came before the executive council last summer, when they reviewed the general case and presented argument regarding the export rate on grain. It will be noted that the executive council directed the attention of the Railway Commission to the fact that further argument had been made in regard to rates on grain, and asking that the railway board review the argument.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is the minister aware of the fact that the province has requested the Railway Commission to hear a further appeal?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think we will meet that situation. The executive council was anxious that there should be an early reference to the Railway Commission in order that, if a reduction were made, the shippers of grain would be able to take advantage of it in the shipping season.
A further reference was made to the railway board by the executive council on the 24th October 1923. I quote the following from it:
One of the main grounds of appeal dealt with on the argument was that regarding the export grain rates from points in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to Vancouver and other British Columbia coast points. This matter has been specifically dealt with by order in council of the 2nd October, 1923 (P.C. 2007).
The committee, therefore, recommends that all other subjects of complaint referred to in the said petition be also remitted to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada to be dealt with as it may deem proper upon the evidence already adduced and the arguments presented before the board and before Your Excellency in Council.
The committee observes, however, that in view of the vital importance of facilitating the interchange of commodities between the various sections of Canada railway rates should be maintained at as low a basis as possible having regard to all proper considerations Accordingly the committee is of the opinion that in the future, should transportation and traffic conditions so change as to render practicable a nearer approach 
to equalization of rates as between prairie and Pacific territory, the board should in the exercise of its discretion take such action as may be necessary to bring about this result.
I have reviewed briefly the reduction that has taken place not only on grain rates but on class rates generally through the appeal made in 1922 and the action of the railway companies in their granting a reduction of 20 per cent, following the order of the board in 1922, and the further reduction granted by the Railway Commission last year on the representations made to them by counsel. As the matter stands to-day the Railway Board of Canada still have before them for consideration the advisability of further reductions in railway rates. In my opinion, with a proper development of our agricultural industry and of our natural resources in the West, further representations will be made to our railways from time to time in the interests of development, and in the not far distant future the discrimination that exists between British Columbia and Alberta will be finally wiped out.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is the minister aware that the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners has refused to hear counsel on behalf of British Columbia in pursuance of the order of the Privy Council?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I imagine that counsel from British Columbia or any province can, under a proper mode of procedure, present arguments to the Board of Railway Commissioners. I did not understand that there had been a refusal to hear further argument, but I am satisfied that if it is the desire to present argument, there is a procedure to be followed to that end.
I wish also to deal with a matter that is of some importance to western Canada as well as to the people of the East. Over a period of many years there has been an agitation on the part of British Columbia that the ocean route be made available for the transport of commodities from the East to the West. These representations have been made by public bodies in the form of petitions from time to time. Last year interest centred around a shipment of steel rails from Sydney, Nova Scotia, which was transshipped at New York for Vancouver. It is suggested that the local customs officer at Sydney indicated verbally that rails shipped in that manner would not be subjected to duty, but on arrival at Vancouver the Dominion customs officer informed the purchaser that goods so shipped would be liable to the same duty as if they had been manufactured in and shipped from the

The Address-Mr. King (Kootenay)
United States. This shipment being rather large and involving a considerable sum of money, very urgent representations were made to the Dominion government by the province of British Columbia. The Dominion government was impressed by the desirability of enabling the people of western Canada as well as of eastern Canada to avail themselves of the cheaper ocean transportation for the movement of Canadian goods. It has been decided that an officer will be placed in New York who will there clear goods in transit for western Canadian ports and also goods coming from western ports to eastern Canadian points. But in the order making provisions for an officer at New York the government have thought it wise to stipulate that goods so moved should be placed in British bottoms, that is, ships of British or Canadian register. It is hoped that by this provision there will be established sailings of British or Canadian ships from Canadian Atlantic ports which will fully accommodate this traffic.

that lines will be established if there are goods to be carried, and we have reason to believe that there will be a very considerable amount of business offering, because it is within the knowledge of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) that no less than two, and possibly three, lines are prepared to enter into this traffic.

There will be a
customs officer at New York and goods shipped to that point will have an opportunity of entering into ships of British registry.
