My question is, why not
other ships?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think it only
fit and proper that we should endeavour to keep this trade within Canadian channels. It will travel over Canadian railways to Canadian ports and will there enter into ships of our own register or of British register to be transported. We are satisfied that in the British merchant marine we have facilities which are sufficiently extensive to give accommodation and to bring about a competition which will control rates in the matter of this tonnage.
I regret to say that one important public body in Vancouver has taken exception to this ruling and contends that these goods should enter ships of any registry and be allowed to move freely. Now, as a representative of British Columbia and a Canadian I do not agree with this contention. I think it absolutely essential, if we are to grow as a nation, that we develop and maintain our national ports. No maritime nation can afford to build up the ports of an adjoining country at the expense of its own. I am satisfied that the people of British Columbia as a whole will endorse this attitude. I am sure that if the position were reversed and the people of Alberta and central British Columbia were to find it more acceptable to ship their goods via the ports of Seattle and Portland, our friends of the Vancouver Board of Trade would be the first to take exception and to insist on certain restrictions that would tend to confine this business to our own ports.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is the government in possession of any assurances to make certain that the nature of that arrangement does not mean that the rates by water will be adjusted somewhat on the same basis and at the same rate as by rail in which case the advantages of going via New York would be virtually nullified so far as lower rates are concerned.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The government will always have it within their power to amend that regulation if it is found that the people who are going to engage in this business are trying to make excessive profits out of it; but primarily, I think, we are on safe ground. It is the policy of this government to develop our own national ports, and this business, which I believe is going to become of very great importance not only to our people in western Canada but I think of even greater importance to our manufacturing friends in central and eastern Canada, should certainly remain in the channels where the
The Address-Mr. Hoey

people of Canada will derive the most benefit from it.
In closing, I wish to say that so far as the people of British Columbia are concerned they are desirous of seeing brought into effect by this parliament policies that will be for the development of the whole of Canada and for the benefit of all the people. We are desirous of seeing a united Canada, where there will be no suggestion of sectional discrimination as between the East and the West. We as a people are desirous of seeing a united Canada grow and prosper and become a great nation, and I believe that with the great natural resources this country possesses and with the people who are known as Canadians to-day, we have a great future before us, a future which will mean much to the Canadian people, a future within the great Empire which we are desirous to see remain as a unit not only for the benefit of British citizenship, but for the advantage of the people of the world.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, several speeches have been delivered during the course of this debate, the very nature of which indicated considerable study and research on the part of those responsible for their creation. There was one speech, however, that seems to have left an indelible impression upon my mind, and to that speech I should like to refer at the outset. It was the speech delivered by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), the gentleman who sits to my extreme right on this bench. Viewed from the standpoint of political progress the speech was refreshing. To me it was stimulating. It was delivered in a spirit wholly non-partisan, and I should like to congratulate the hon. member upon the delivery of that speech. His was a voice from the wilderness, it is true, but nevertheless a voice I think in which we all detected very pronounced modem and progressive accents. It was significant to me, and must have been significant to others, that while one of the oldest members of this chamber, and I trust he will not think I am speaking disrespectfully, spoke in that tone, one of its youngest members of his party the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), declared very eloquently and very emphatically, and in his own inimitable style, that he still believed in and stood for the policy that has now reached or almost reached its allotted span.
Might I add this to what the hon. member for South York so ably said? I sometimes feel almost instinctively that we are in the very presence of a new organization of human society on a co-operative rather than a competitive basis. I do not mean by that that
(Mr. J. H. King.l
we are going to witness any violent social upheavals, anything of a cataclysmic nature, but I do feel that we are in the grip of forward moving forces. Furthermore, I believe that Great Britain to-day is becoming the very spearhead of the forces that labour for the triumph of democracy and modern civilization. I recall to mind at the moment a statement that fell from the lips of a very distinguished American citizen immediately after the close of the Great War. Addressing thousands of his fellow-countrymen who had come to hear him, he said:
World civilization during the last four years has been passing through a revolution, a revolution which for magnitude of destruction is unparalleled in the history of human endeavour. The old social order has collapsed, and all attempts to restore it on the traditional competitive basis will end in disappointment and in disillusionment.
The discussion during the course of this debate has centred around and at times merged wholly in the question of the customs tariff. It seemed to me as I listened to the addresses delivered in defence of the protective principle, that I could detect in them all, indeed almost in every sentence, the same fallacy, a fallacy, Mr. Speaker, that in my judgment is going to influence many in this country and confuse the issue until it is successfully exploded. I refer to the fallacy of looking upon production as an end in itself, rather than as a means to an end, and that the enrichment of the Canadian people. I refer to that pernicious fallacy of looking upon labour, regardless of the expenditure of human energy, as something to be desired and something to be provided, regardless of the expense of that labour to the nation. Let me illustrate what I mean. A few weeks ago we had an abundance of snow in the city of Ottawa. That snow provided work for a certain number of men ordinarily unemployed. They were paid for the services rendered out of the pockets of the tax-payers of this city. Had that snow not come those men could have been paid an equal amount, perhaps more, in working on constructive enterprises and the citizens of Ottawa would have stood to benefit in that they would have been saved from the slush and irritation associated in our minds with life in the Dominion capital a few weeks ago. Had this money not been spent in that way it could have been devoted to constructive enterprises with the return of spring. And so it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we have reached this stage: The protectionist prays continually for more snow, the free-trader for the return of spring and the release of natural forces. This brings me to the end of the first section of my remarks, and if the House has no objection I should

The Address-Mr. Hoey
feel thankful, Mr. Speaker, if you would call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
When the House took recess
at six o'clock I was dealing with what I described to be a pernicious policy, a policy that looked upon labour or production as an end in itself, rather than as a means to an end, a policy which if persisted in would have us destroy Canadian buildings and abolish modern machineiy in an attempt to provide employment. As a further illustration of what I have in mind, I want to quote some figures. During the years 1915 to 1918 inclusive a certain factory in this country produced 113,542 automobiles, and the excess price charged to Canadian purchasers over the prevailing price in the United States was $13,394,941. The wages paid by that concern during that period on the cars actually made and sold in Canada amounted to $9,083,360, and their total wage $11,960,807. That is their total wage bill on cars made for sab. in Canada and for export. They paid in taxes during that period $2,284,145, leaving a surplus of $2,027,436. What do these figures mean? They mean that during this period the people of Canada could have paid all the wages this firm paid, all the taxes this firm paid, and had a surplus in the national treasury of $2,027,436, or a sum sufficient in itself to pay more than half the duty paid by this firm on their raw material entering into the manufacture of this article. The honourable, unassuming and genial member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) during the course or his speech a few days ago, told a st">ry the point of which I failed to get at the moment. The story was that of a boy, the son of a religiously-inclined mother, and the boy was anxious to secure a drum. He punctuated his evening prayer with a request for this drum, and when he received it he proved ungrateful. Just what relationship exists between a drum and those who demand free trade I could not detect. Those who advocate free trade advocate it not for themselves but for all. It is a doctrine of freedom as opposed to a doctrine of slavery. But I want to tell the story of a boy, not the son of a religiously-inclined mother, and not the son of a woman of questionable character, but the son of a mother who was described by all as an incurable flirt, particularly when in association
with politicians. She was consequently a very popular women, particularly with the older politicians. This woman had several boys, but I want to refer tu one of them in particular. His name vas called Industry Infant Industry. Just why he should have been given that name no one seemed to know. There were those, however, who contended that the name was given him by one Macdonald, a Scotchman, who declared that ultimately the boy would grow and discard that name; that is to say, he would, ultimately grow up and finally be knighted Viscount Monopoly. The boy was natural to begin with, but because of the position in which he was inclined to sit he developed spinal trouble-spinal meningitis. He became obsessed with a very unnatural obsession-
I presume all obsessions are unnatural-an obsession that the littie children with whom he played from day to day sought his destruction, and so he became persistent in his demands for a gun. Night after night, as his mother would attempt to teach him the evening prayer he would punctuate it thus-
Now I lay me down to sleep-
("I want a gun")
I pray the Lord my soul to keep.
("I want a gun")
If I should die before I wake-
("I want a gun")
I pray the Lord my soul to take.
("Get me that gun!")
And finally the gun was provided. He woke in the morning, and, instead of proving grateful, he looked at it and said, "Where the devil did that toy gun come from? I want a gun, that will not only enable me to shoot those American kids next door, but those Italian kids that live at the end of the avenue, and those German kids who live on Kitchener street, and those English kids that live across the way." I think my hon. and genial friend from Brantford will agree with me that it is a dangerous thing to put guns in the hands of children, particularly children who seek the destruction of their fellows. The Canadian Manufacturers, that august body, at a meeting recently held in Hamilton passed a resolution which I shall read to the House. It is the very embodiment of modesty and reads-
The adoption of a stable and sound fiscal policy, based on an adequate customs tariff, will bind together more firmly the provinces of Canada in national unity, attract capital, commercialize natural resources, strengthen existing industries and create new industries, raise revenue, encourage immigration, provide employment, increase traffic through national ports, furnish passengers and freight for transportation systems, lower freight rates; make farming more profitable by pro-

The Address-Mr. Hoey
viding new markets abroad and facilitate profitable bargaining by means of tariffs with other countries.
I said that that was the very embodiment of modesty, because it leaves out two very important factors. It should have added unlimited campaign funds and political preferment for the party willing to espouse it. Indeed, I do not know but that they might have legitimately claimed that if you elevate the tariff high enough, that is from the low plane upon which it now is, up higher and higheT and higher, it will ultimately restore hair and thus protect the bald heads of those who advocate it. You can imagine then the embarrassing position in which the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) would find himself as opposed to that in which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) would find himself. That is the difficulty with the tariff. It never evenly distributes the benefits that accrue therefrom.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens)-let me say with respect to him that I am just as anxious to lead him from the error of his ways as he is to lead me from the pathway of rectitude-during the course of a speech which he delivered, and with which I shall deal, deprecated the tendency in some quarters to speak of the principle of protection as an immoral principle.
I do not know that it is altogether accurate to speak of any economic principle in the abstract as immoral. It is, perhaps, not immoral as an abstract economic principle, but, in my judgment, it is immoral and vicious in its results. You ask, why? A system of taxation that slaps the mother in the face for every child that is bom into the world by adding a tax on the woollen garments with which she would clothe it; a system of taxation that takes eight .times as much out of the pockets of the mechanic with eight of a family who is earning $100 a month as it takes out of the pockets of a bachelor with the same wages; a system of taxation that has always led to monopoly, to centralization of wealth and the impoverishment of the rural districts, the only source from which national life can be renewed,-why should we hesitate to speak of the results which accrue from protection as immoral? The evils of protection are as wide-spread as the territory in which it operates, as deep as the distress into which our people have fallen, and for which it is in no small measure responsible. Then, having spoken of the tendency to speak of the principle of protection as immoral, he went on to speak of the woollen industry. I have no objection to a man defending the woollen industry or any other industry, provided that [Mr. Hoey.)	I
in so doing he does not attempt to pull the wool over the hon. members' eyes. He spoke of the condition in which the woollen industry finds itself to-day. Every one that is truly Canadian-and we are all truly Canadian- regrets that condition, and if that condition in itself had not been productive of compensating factors, it would be a catastrophe. He spoke of the number of skilled workers that were thrown out of employment, skilled workers that could not easily be replaced. I want to be fair; but it was news to me to learn that the modern woollen industry, with which I am more or less familiar, required workers to be trained over a period of years in order to operate successfully modern machinery. Let us, however, suppose that that is true, and that those workers cannot be replaced from Great Britain or from any other country. Let us suppose that they are trekking to the United States, as he contended they were, to the extent of one thousand. What about the agriculturists to-day who are leaving the land, agriculturists who have been anchored to the soil for generations, experienced men? Is this not even a greater loss? I have before me the figures, provided by the United States Department of Immigration, showing not only the number of Canadians who entered the United States during the year 1923, but classifying them:
Canadians entering the United States.
Year ending June 30,	July,	August,1923	1923	1923Weavers and spinners..	.. 426	54	48Farm labourers	.. 3,295	422	454Bona fide farmers.. ..	.. 5,409	827	697
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre compared wages paid in this country with wages paid in Great Britain. I did not think the comparison was altogether fair, for this reason, that comparing wages paid in Canada with wages paid in Great Britain means nothing unless you determine accurately and scientifically the purchasing power of the dollar. He did not, however, fall into the old trap, the trap into which protectionists sometimes fall, but which was very carefully avoided by him, that is the trap that protection is of itself responsible for keeping up wages, because during this discussion he admitted that the wages in the woollen industry were due, not to protection, but to a statute passed by the Ontario government. This admission is in itself an evidence that the tariff does not of its own volition keep up wages. How can the woollen industry be helped? The woollen industry can be helped, it seems to me, by reducing the cost of living, by substantial all-round reductions in the customs

The Address-Mr. Hoey
tariff, by releasing the natural resources and energy of this nation, and thus enabling us to build up industries that are truly indigenous. Without attempting to argue that two wrongs make a right, I want to compare the condition in which the woollen industry finds itself to-day with the condition of the province and the people of the province from which I come, a province with a population of almost 700,000 people. The provincial treasurer in his annual budget declared that the gross value of Manitoba's crops this year amounted to some 855,000,000; but I have in my hand a statement made out by the president of the Winnipeg Board of Trade, which goes to show that if you deduct threshing costs, elevator charges and transportation expenses you will find that the wheat, oats, barley, rye and flax crop of Manitoba this year amounted to 826,280,000 net. The total taxes amounted to 852,255,000. Let us take the estimate of the provincial treasurer that the gross value of the crop amounted to 855,000,000. It only meets our tax burden obligations which amount to 852,-
255,000.	What about our private obligations, what about our cost of living, what about tariff taxation that does not reach the national exchequer at all?
When you go to those farmers in Manitoba to-day and inform them that the woollen industry in eastern Canada is in a precarious position despite the fact that they, in common with the rest of the country, have been subsidizing it for forty years, but that if they wil. only decide to pay anywhere between 30 and 50 per cent more for woollen garments and continue to feed the employees in the industry at a price less than the cost of production, then they will have the advantage of witnessing the upgrowth of the woollen industry in the Dominion, naturally, our farmers are dissatisfied. But when we come down here and attempt to bring some measure of relief to the people we have the honour to represent, our actions are described as indicating "indecent haste!" Of course, you should not be in a hurry to relieve people whose taxes this year are double their revenue; that would not be seemly. Not only are our actions described as indicating indecent haste, but we are accused of "political intrigue"-whatever that means-working beneath the surface of things, entering into unholy alliances; and by the press we are taunted with being more interested in our indemnities than we are in the people. Well, is there a member in this House who, if he is honest, will not admit that he is interested in his indemnity? But these charges are
directed against us, not because hon. members believe them to be true. Deep down in their hearts they know such charges are false. They have not the slightest doubt in their minds with respect to our sincerity. This is mere political camouflage in an attempt to discredit us and build up the shattered remnants of the party to which they belong.
During the course of this debate we have been assured that Canada is in serious danger of being inundated with a superfluous; quantity of wealth; it is threatening to overflow the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific and the flood is coming from even' conceivable quarter. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) does not fear the United States so much, but he has a holy horror of Germany and France and Italy. Surely these nations, because of the government's action with respect to the tariff during the last two years, are dumping goods into [DOT] this country out of all proportion to what they ought to be permitted to send us! Well, let us take the case of Germany for the last two years. In 1922 we imported from Germany goods to the value of $2,041,016; we exported 84,409,547 worth. Not much evidence there of any inundation of wealth. In 1923-nine months-we imported from that country goods to the value of 84,115,295, and we exported 810,455,556 worth., -The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) was alarmed lest we should be flooded with French wines. Let us look at the imports from France. In 1922 they amounted in value to 813,482,005, and we exported 88,208,228 worth. In 1923-nine months-after that iniquitous treaty, we imported goods to the value of 811,749,515, and we exported over
813,865,000	worth. Let us look at the case of Italy. I think I remember the hon. member for North Waterloo referred to Italy. In 1922 we imported from that country goods to the value of $1,387,370; we exported 815,335,818 worth. Let us take nine months of 1923: we imported from Italy goods to the value of 81,430,284-let us keep our minds on the millions-and we exported 817,445,158 worth.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I want to turn to that perennial argument-the home market. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre during the course of his remarks turned himself completely in this direction. He admitted that he could not hope his thoughts would enter our heads-the natural inference I drew was that our heads at least were not empty-but nevertheless he discussed the home market. I do not want to be too severe, I do not want to indulge in castigations, but I must frankly
The Address-Mr. Hoey

state that I do not believe for a moment the hon. member expected us to take him seriously. I say that because I have too great respect for his intelligence and for his practical knowledge of modem business and its intricacies to think for a moment that he expected us either to take him seriously or to accept his arguments. Now, what were his arguments? Briefly they were these: That the Dominion of Canada should look forward to a time, by steadily developing and building up the home market, when it could practically absorb-not wholly but practically, absorb-all the wheat produced in this country. I hope this is a fair statement of his case, because I do not wish to misrepresent him.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me to observe that that is not a fair statement of my case?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is exceedingly difficult to know just what a fair representation of his case would be; but that, in my judgment, was the position in general terms, that he took; that was the impression left upon my mind and, I think, upon the minds of those with whom I associate in this section of the House. I want to point out to the government, and -1 do so in all seriousness, that if this is the policy the Conservative party in this country intend to pursue, either in the immediate or in the distant future, then that fact in itself ought to have a tremendous influence upon certain expenditures that the government are about to make, and the first of these expenditures is with respect to the development of the harbour at Vancouver. The hon. member does not believe in the importation of goods into this country-that is a view to which I shall refer in a moment- and he looks forward to the time when there will be no necessity to ship wheat from Canada in large quantities. Then what in the name of Heaven do they want a harbour at Vancouver for? Do they want it for the incubation of mermaids? Do they want a modem pool of Siloam out there for washing and cleansing discredited politicians? I want to say that I was interested in the developments at Vancouver. I discussed the matter at some length with the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), whose firm contemplates making certain expenditures there. But if I believed that either in the immediate or in the remote future Canada was apt to absorb her own wheat crop, then I would absolutely speak against and vote against this appropriation.

Not only are we contemplating expenditures at Vancouver-and I trust that the people at Vancouver will grasp the significance of the philosophy that is being disseminated in and from this Chamber by their representative-not only are we attempting to build up harbour facilities there, but we are seriously considering the most pretentious and certainly the most costly project ever contemplated by the people of this country, the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. For what purpose? In order to facilitate the transportation of grain, not only during the immediate future but for a century, perhaps, to come. Well, if you look forward to the time when this country ought to consume its own wheat-and I put this seriously to the Prime Minister and to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb); I can see evidences of interest in his countenance-if the policy advocated by my hon. friend has even a * semblance of truth, then why not spend the money that you are going to spend at Van-couvcer and that you are thinking of spending on the St. Lawrence-why not spend it in dumping immigrants into this country? That is the logical outcome; that is the point to which his reasoning must lead us.
Oh, of course he would let certain goods come into this country. He did not specify them, so I can only imagine just what goods he would let in. He is opposed to the importation of French wines. I have thought the matter over and I presume that he would not be opposed to bringing balloons into this country. Then visualize for yourself six or seven ocean liners sailing along the deepened St. Lawrence, loaded with balloons for western Canada! Of course he would let raw material into this country-raw material from where? From the countries where there is cheap labour and where they could turn it into the finished article more cheaply than we could. Of course he will argue that he does not look forward to a time when we shall be wholly able to consume our own wheat, and that leads us back exactly to where the United States is to-day, a country that last year exported a litttle less than one-tenth of its wheat. It leads us back to the position not only of the agriculturists in the United States but to the railroads in the United States, many of which are almost bankrupt. Mr. Speaker, I challenge absolutely and positively his statement that the power of consumption of wheat in modern civilization is static at 650,000,000 bushels. The best English statisticians, the best English economists, assure us to-day that wheat consumption in Europe is one-third below normal. If you exercise your reasoning

The Address-Mr. Hoey
faculties for a moment, you can easily understand that on a continent where thousands are out of employment, where there is destitution and squalor and poverty, particularly in the protected countries over there, wheat consumption is in no sense normal, and if in Europe it has been static over a period of years, that condition has been due to the shattered purchasing power of the European nations. While the number of wheat consumers in modem civilization cannot be increased-not by acts of parliament-you can immeasurably increase their capacity to consume. A question was put by the hon. member for Battleford (Mr. McConica), and it was this: If you bring ten millions of people from Europe and put them in this country, do you not deplete Europe's consumption power? The question, Mr. Speaker, was not answered, because in my judgment it is absolutely unanswerable, and I think I can explain why. Although it was not answered, that does not mean that the hon. member did not make an honest attempt, finding himself in an awkward position, to reply to it, and I thought as I sat here quietly and thoughtfully, what an ingenious answer! First he said that the people drawn from such countries would not necessarily be drawn from wheat consuming nations. Now, if he had not put in the term "Europe" there I would have said that he had become converted and that he was in favour of bringing orientals to this country, but I cannot believe that. Well, if he does not belive in bringing in orientals, can he tell me a nation in Europe that is not a wheat consuming nation?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, lots of them.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is not in Europe, Mr. Speaker, a single nation the people of which do not consume wheat, and to stand up in this room and contend that there is is an insult to the intelligence of the men sitting here. That term "wheat consuming country" is occasionally used in the grain trade. It is a misnomer; it is a meaningless term in the grain trade, and it has no place here. When it is used in the grain trade it is used to denote countries that consume wheat, but do not import wheat. Let us suppose that we import from Russia five million people into this country. You increase the consumption here, of course, but you deplete the con sumption in Russia, and thus enable Russia to put that much more wheat on the Liverpool market.
The second explanation given was this, and it is perhaps more ingenious still. The second answer-shall I call it an evasion?-
was this: That the exodus of people from Europe to the United States or to Australia or any other country is more than offset by the increase in population. I have not examined the figures; I did not think it worth while. But if those people did not leave Europe at all, would not the population increase? To say that the exodus of people from a country, or the mere distribution of the population, by emigration or immigration, has anything at all to do with the gradual propagation of the race is positively absurd. Look where the reasoning leads. Here is a young man in England thinking of getting married and he says to his sweetheart: "I think we can get married now because I saw by the papers the other day that several carloads of people have left for Canada." That is the conclusion to which you are driven; there is no escape from it. I will admit this:	The
hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson) is here. He has read and studied along this line a great deal more than I have. I do not know that he is a Malthusian, but I know that he has studied quite a lot of Malthusian works. I will admit that economic factors to-day have some influence on the propagation of the race, particularly amongst the better-off people, but certainly economic conditions have no influence on the propagation of the race amongst the great masses of European peasants from whom we draw our immigrant population. And so it seems to me that we are brought back to the position in which the United States finds itself to-day, that is, we cannot positively hope to build up the home market to a greater extent than they have built it up.
The hon. member fell into the same fallacy again when he referred to the one thousand employees in the woollen industry who had trekked to the United States and ceased to consume wheat in Canada. Of course, but they trekked into the United States to consume wheat there, and to the extent that they consume it there they will reduce the exportable surplus of the United States to Liverpool.
Now in reply to an interrogation with respect to the United States the hon. member attributed the position of that country to two factors: First to the fact that the United States was an exporter of grain, and second, to the depletion of the soil in that country of its plant food content. Now that is the exact position to which we are drifting in this country, to the depletion of our soil of plant food content. This is the effect in the Prairie West:
The effect of a generation of cropping to wheat has been to reduce the nitrogen of the surface seven inches
The Address-Mr. Hoey

The Address- Mr. Hoey

tannia", and as their closing hymn "God save the King", and choose as their text, "Buy only made-in-Canada goods", and who, if they were straightforward, would declare to their hearers during their sermons " As far as the East is from the West, so far have we removed your possessions from you". Loyalists, shall I call these men? They remind me of those bats that inhabit certain caves in Kentucky, of which scientists speak, bats that love darkness rather than light. Because they chose darkness, nature has robbed them of their power to see,-not of their eyes, their eyes remain, but they have lost their power of vision. There are other ways and means, but let me say that if the British preference were drastically increased to draw imports this way, what would be the effect upon Russia? Would she not still continue to be a competitor? She would. But with our cost of production reduced here, we would have a chance of competing successfully with her. But there is another factor. If the drastic increases in the British preference took place immediately, the tendency in Russia would be to go in more for diversified farming rather than wheat growing. The stage of her development lends itself to that form of agriculture, and frankly I cannot see the sense or reason of shipping live stock from Alberta or Saskatchewan to Great Britain; we cannot do it profitably, while at the same time they are shipping wheat from Russia to Britain. Why not have a reversal of the order of things? Why not, by a rearrangement of trade, ship wheat from Canada, and have live stock shipped from Russia? There are other ways and means that can be evolved; not only can the cost of production be brought down by legislation, but it can be brought down by co-operative effort. I want to say with respect to the co-operative project that it is on its way in western Canada at the present time. Whether it is successful or not, never did the western agriculturist attempt anything more worthy of him, never did the western agriculturist attempt anything more in keeping with the spirit and demands of the age, never did he attempt anything more ethical than when he attempted, as he is attempting now, to take this staple commodity from the producer and place it on the table of the consumer without enhancing its price by the superfluous intervention of unnecessary middlemen. I want to say that there are certain compulsory features about the present wheat pool that I dislike, but let me express'the hope that, in the course of time, those compulsory features will be relegated to the scrap heap, and that this pool will go on until it can establish a relationship 
between the co-operative exporting institutions in the Old Country. What could be more natural than that this great co-operative pool, marketing her commodity to the extent of $400,000,000 annually, should ultimately establish relationships between co-operative organizations in the Old Country? I think it would establish those relationships now were it not for the tariff barriers that keep British commodities from this country at the present time.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask a question?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I understand from the hon. member's statement that he is in favour of the British preference. I ask then how could he consistently say that, if he is not in favour also of tariffs against other countries? Because a preference, I would say, must assume that there shall be a tariff? You cannot have a preference unless there is a tariff.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My reply to that thoughtful question is simply this, that I am dealing with conditions as they are,-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is what I was doing.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fully realise the disadvantage, which I must bear as cheerfully as I can, the pronounced contrast, of having it fall to my lot to follow a speaker so very entertaining as he who has just resumed his seat. That hon. gentleman (Mr. Hoey) certainly combines five or six very valid factors which constitute him easily one of the most acceptable speakers in this parliament. Whether or not to-night he was in possession of that moderation which is almost always so characteristic of him, I will say this, that all his aggressiveness and all his pointed, but unpoisoned, humour were more than justified in exposing the immoderateness of the position of the "neck Or nothing" high protectionist in this country and in this House. In so far as they represent some small wing of public opinion-
25i
and I say this in kindliness-they are to-night a distinct barrier across the path of all the major numbers of true and patriotic Canadians who are looking for some honourable compromise upon this crucial question of the tariff.
Hon. members in this House are generous as to the latitude, range and scope of topics which they call in order in this particular discussion, and I hope my remarks, perhaps rather rambling, will be at least technically in order, and I also hope, for the good of my auditors, that they shall not be of undue length.	I did not hear, but I read the
speech of my colleague, the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan). He reviewed with his masterly fidelity the rights and aspirations of the Maritimes, a question and a subject which may possibly appear to stale a little on the ear of those in this part of the Dominion, but which is still dear to us and a matter of trust. The hon. gentleman did so well that I do not propose to review what he reviewed with a masterful hand, except to refer to one subject, unimportant, perhaps, in one sense, and yet important in another sense, a subject which relates to the honourable and successful management of our great National Railways in this country. In my home town, which is a strong railway town, there are to-night three old employees of that road, who were old employees of the Intercolonial, and they stand under the stain of a dismissal by this railway board. The charges include irregularities and the grave claim that these men were pilfering money which they took from passengers by way of railway fares. I need scarcely say that if the charges were true, such a man would deserve little or no consideration. I need however, scarcely say that it will be a truism to every lawyer at least in this House that on a charge so serious the proof should be absolutely satisfactory and convincing and obtained in a thoroughly judicial way. These men are men of splendid reputations, men with such a standing in their community that those who know them would be sorry to believe they would do a single thing that was wrong. I read over the typed evidence in the case of the investigation which resulted in one dismissal, and I found that the method of trailing these men was to put spotters, as you may contemptuously call them, or detectives, if you prefer the more dignified term, upon their trail, and upon their train to clandestinely watch their actions, to see if the appropriate document was punched and handed to the passenger in cases where the latter did not obtain a ticket at the railway depot. They

The Address-Mr. Putnam
made their investigation like wolves, in a pack, and claimed that they found that some of these old and honoured conductors had held back and appropriated fares. The principle is the same, whatever the amount involved. Well, Sir, at that investigation only one of the detectives appeared and manfully faced the conductor whom he had accused. In the case of the other spotters, though they, the deponents were not there, their bald affidavits were used to convict and dismiss the accused.
That is the state of affairs we have there, the railway board hiring these detectives to trail the conductors, securing from them affidavits to do their cowardly work while the deponents were shooed away. Instead of having every accuser face the accused, with the right for each to look the other in the eye, and for the conductor or his friend or his counsel to cross-examine his accuser, and so enable the investigator to judge of the credibility of the opposing witnesses-because the conductors denied the charge-and make a judicial finding, we have the condition I have described.
I complained of the action to high officials of the board, including Sir Henry Thornton himself. I received an answer from them and from him which was neither satisfactory nor judicial in its tone, and I find it my duty, as the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has found it his duty, to put this matter before parliament. I hope no hon. member will say that this business is unimportant, and that the owner of no heart is so callous that he would advise us to go back to the board, and if we cannot get justice there, that that is the end of it. The management of this great system of railways by a board of directors is as yet in its infancy and upon trial, and the board itself is but a child of this administration, indeed of this parliament, and therefore I ask the sympathy and the interest of hon. members in this connection. Surely we are spending money enough on a large legal staff to advise the board in all the intricacies of its work wherein questions of law or equity arise, and I hope these highly paid legal experts will be able to build up a proper British system for investigating any alleged wrong-doing by the employees of the road. It may be said that an employer has the right to dismiss his employee. But these cases are not parallel with the ordinary case. Where an individual or private firm dismisses an employee he suffers no public injustice, there is no undue publicity, and the man can go off and, whether guilty or innocent, has a fair chance to (Mr. Putnam.]
get a living at some other work; but to dismiss an old and honoured conductor of a publicly-owned railroad casts suspicion upon him all over the country, and he has no chance of recovering his reputation for honesty or of securing some other employment. Worse still, in this case the railway board say the dismissed conductor shall have no claim to any benefits of the pension fund to which he has contributed for many years and in absolute good faith. I say that these men should have a new trial, or get the benefit of the substantial doubt that exists and be restored to their positions; or that at worst their pension rights should be restored to them.
As a Nova Scotian, Mr. Speaker, I feel a sense of sorrow for the illness which is responsible for the absence from this House of the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). The reports from his residence concerning his health are, I believe, decidedly cheering. We know that he is paying the penalty for having exerted his patriotic energy too long after that gcod grey head which all men know became white with the blossoms of the almond tree We do trust, in fact we have a lively hope, that even this session he is going to be with us for a while. We all sincerely hope that, restored to all the health which might be expected of one in his somewhat advanced years, he will long enjoy a period of comparative rest wherein this country shall still have the benefit of his courageous and sane optimism and of his ripe experience am* sage advice.
I equally regret that the hand of illness is upon the ex-Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin). Fortunately his illness does not seem to be so severe and we have the prospect of seeing him back with us very soon in this House.' The hon member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) the other night indulged in a joke by relating an anecdote to the effect that when the ex-minister was asked how he was, he said he was sick, but not half so sick as when he was administering his department. Well Sir, I think we could name two or three at least of the fifty hon. members in the Conservative group who would not feel the least bit sick if they saw the slightest possibility of succeeding to the portfolio of the Minister of Justice. But whether the country at iarge would not have some qualms of conscience and some warning qualms of the stomach in the happening of such an event I think is entirely another question.

The Address-Mr. Putnam
I was led to reflect on the record thus far of our new Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when I heard the magnificent speech to which he treated us the other afternoon, and I am sure that in him the Liberal party and the country at large have found a worthy successor to his immediate and distinguished predecessor. Higher compliment I could not pay.
As a comparatively new member in this House, I want to personally welcome those who have taken their seats here since last session. I do that without prejudice to my view of. the fallacy of the cause which may have sent a couple of them here. In the case of the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Doucet)
I agree with the talented member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) that the newcomer exhibited no nervousness in the making of his maiden speech. But I think he should be congratulated upon his good fortune in not having his fire returned by hon. members who sit around me on this side of the House, because I must say that he made a very questionable use of the white flag in prefacing his remarks by a request that we accord him the concession of consideration because it was his maiden effort, and then proceeding to launch an attack upon us which, to put it very mildly, was not as free from partisan extravagance as he was physically free himself from the demon of nervousness. But, Mr. Speaker, I notice he has left his seat, and therefore I shall refrain from half a dozen other observations which I intended to make respecting his initial speech m this chamber.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in the course of his contribution to this debate put on a very earnest look-and I assume he was really earnest- and said that there was a distinct impression of anxiety throughtout the business world of the Dominion as to an impression that we were actually going to reduce the tariff. Well, he may call it anxiety in the business world, but I would call it a rattling of the dry bones of those infant industries which, with nearly forty-six years over their heads, refuse to grow up and stand alone.
I was interested in the speech of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) the other day. The hon. member has an honourable military record and I am entirely sincere in congratulating him on that. The hand that for our country fought, whether it grasped a sword, whether it helped to heal the wounded, whether it ministered to those who died in battle-harness, is a hand I hope that as a citizen of this country I shall always properly honour. But my only regret is that the hon. member from that constituency is by no means as good a statesman as he is a warrior. He made an exceedingly partisan speech from the purely Conservative standpoint. One illustration he took to prove that the Conservative party was actually more democratic than the Liberal party was this: He said that we should go to the country; that his party went to the country when they had a majority of twenty-five over all. Well, many a bankrupt has quite a showing of goods in his shop, and the way to get at his real condition is to foot up his liabilities and his assets. They had that asset of twenty-five or thirty members and they had this liability facing them: just as often as they opened a constituency _ they would lose it by an overwhelming majority that indicated unmistakably the feeling of the people. I think the picture of Medicine Hat was one of the last that came into their dreams; and then, like a man doomed to cross a river where the ice was thin, they got into that state where they did not know whether it was safer to go on or to turn back. They actually opened another county; they spent the people's money in issuing the writs, in engaging a returning officer and in getting the machinery ready. But all this was done as a camouflage with regard to the time of bringing on the general election; either that, or it was done in a state of hysteria when they did not know their own mind. Well, that by-election had scarcely got under way when it was submerged by the larger issues of a general election. Yes, they had a majority of twenty-five or thirty when they went to the country. I am reminded of an occasion when I was out in a boat on Cobequid bay, a branch of the Bay of Fundy. Joseph Howe once told the people of Nova Scotia to boast of their province, that if they could say nothing else for it they could say that it had the highest tides in the world I am a poor sailor, and I found myself in a small, frail boat at the flood tide, with too many in it even for calm weather. The conditions were such that our lives were actually in danger. Not far away from us was a sand bar a few acres in extent which was rapidly becoming covered by the stormy water. A little girl in the boat pleaded with her father to run the boat over to that island in the sand, which, as all except her knew, would within an hour be entirely submerged by the tide. Of course we did not take that advice; we made for the shore, and by good luck we got there. These gentlemen do not deserve any particular thanks for choosing no
The Address-Mr. Putnam

longer to stand upon that majority of twenty-five or thirty, around which there raged the tide of public indignation, but rather to go to the country. They took a chance, as we did, to get to the shore of a new lease of power, and, as history has shown, they went down. But their position with that majority of twenty-five would have been just as untenable and as ridiculous as ours would have been had we disembarked on that little area of sand in the path of the tide.
The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River has told us that what this country needs is a redeclaration of the National Policy. I am sure that anyone who has that idea is behind the age; in fact, Rip Van Winkle himself was up to the minute in comparison with him. A redeclaration of the National Policy? Why, you are going back to something that had more than a fair trial and that was more than a colossal failure. A redeclaration of the National Policy? The country will know that that implies an absolute repudiation and repeal of every vestige of the British preference. I remember the days when the National Policy was dragging on its weary length, when 1 was a young man; like Micawber we were waiting for something to turn up. At every Tory political meeting to which I would go the statement was made that our foreign trade was increasing literally by millions, and this was put forward as a wonderful argument. I to-day took the trouble to get the figures on that, and I find that with eighteen years of trial of the National Policy, from 1S78 until 1896, the total trade of Canada increased from $169,000,000, in round figures, to $221,000,000. That was an increase of about $50,000,000 which was flaunted from every Tory platform in those days and was put forth as proof of the success of .the National Policy. But what was the increase during the next fifteen years under the Lauries' administration, which saw the institution of the important incidence of the British preference? I find that the total trade of Canada increased from $221,000,000 in 1896 to $742,000,000 in 1911, or, roughly, ten times in fifteen years the amount that it had increased in eighteen years under the National Policy when it was functioning under the supervision of its own authors and finishers.
I cannot for the life of me see any reason for turning back the hands of the clock and making a redeclaration of the National Policy. I suppose every one of these forty-six year old infant industries would then want to be rebaptized and to assume the state of newborn babes. I can imagine that in future generations there would be a recurrence of this condition. Suppose the tariff were established

as at the time of the National Policy and there were a gradual policy of attrition in respect to customs duties in response to public dissatisfaction. The future beneficiaries of that wonderful policy would come back to the parliament of that future day and say, "We want a rebaptism; we want a redeclaration of the National Policy; we want a second or third life, a second or third chance." If it were the case of a cat I could conceive of her modesty coming to an end at about the ninth visit, but with the insatiate greed of the high protectionist I am afraid the process would be perpetual.
The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River-and I will give him credit for it-was decidedly original in two or three of his remarks during the course of his address. He told us boldly, and it was a complete reversal of the whole song that we have heard sung by his political associates since the election of 1921, that the country has been plunged into the alleged slough of despond in which it now flounders because, chiefly, we did not carry out our pre-election promises. I think the thing was all the other way. That is, his party that said our promises were utterly unsound and ridiculous and that their fulfilment would be the ruin of this country. It reminds me of the little boy who was asked by his school teacher to write an essay upon Pins, and he proceeded to write a little essay on the subject. His first sentence was: "Pins save thousands of lives." "Why Johnny", said his teacher, "How do you make that out?" "Oh", he says, "it is because people do not swallow them." And I suppose that if the hon. member had lived in Bible times he would have said that the only sure way to compass the death of John the Baptist would have .been for King Herod to deny the dancer when she asked for John's head upon a charger. I say that the avoidance of the fulfilment of our promises, according to the Conservative party, was the salvation of the country.
It makes me just a little bit doubtful in so far as I can keep my mind from confusion in that state of facts, whether after all his heart really turned away from those sound economic propositions which were his when he was advocating that we should accept the proffer of reciprocity from the United States. He tells us that he went back on that, and he quoted Lincoln for his authority. I am afraid his authority was very far drawn. He professes to have seen the light like Paul. I do not think it was sun, moon or stars. It may have been the light that never was on sea or shore; or the light that failed. As for giving
The Address-Mr. Putnam
us any satisfactory answer or any semblance of a reason, he did nothing except to quote Lincoln from this long distance of time. I listened in vain for any real explanation of his somersault.
The hon. gentleman did tell us that we must look to the United States as a great example of the success of protection. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think we have said many times, and I think it is a truism and an axiom, that the United States herself is a great example of the success of free trade. I do not care what technically you call the tariffs which from time to time are found upon her wide walls; she has a great diversity of soil anl clime, f fruit and grain and mineral and fish, of resources vast and varied. She has the advantage of a seaboard that is wonderful. I say that the United States is a great example of the success of free trade. I do not think there is an area in the world which can boast in the same mileage such splendid resources, or such a splendid example of the success of free trade as the United States itself. We cannot adopt any parrot rule and say that because protection is good for the United States it is good for us. Our situation is vastly different, as I would like to show, or rather to review, for every sensible member knows it. The cases are by no means parallel; in fact, they are very dissimilar.
As I said before, the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has so well dealt with the Maritime provinces that I am not going to weary you with that subject, except to quote a few figures of population which I think raise a prima facie case that we were not given a fair deal in the device of confederation. In 1871 the population of Ontario was 1.620,851, and in 1921 it had increased to 2,933,622, or an increase of more than 80 per cent; Quebec's population in 1871 was 1,191,516, and in 1921 it had increased to 2,361,199. or over 100 per cent; Nova Scotia's population in 1871 was 387,800, and in 1921 it had increased to 523,837, or an increase of less than 40 per cent; New Brunswick's population in 1871 was 285,594, and in 1921, 387,876, or an increase of less than 40 per cent; Prince Edward Island's population in 1871 was 94,021, and in 1921 it had decreased to 88,615, or about 5 per cent. Without wearying the House I wish to contrast the difference between the Maritime provinces and the central provinces by this test of increase m population, and I say that on the face of it, it raises the presumption that confederation is economically a comparatively bad thing for us. In putting this claim before you I ask this administration and this parliament to
seek carefully for the remedy, and for the British principle of fair play and of evenhanded justice to all. I was going to make this suggestion, Mr. Speaker:	It is possible
when we find ourselves up against the serious conditions that obtain in this country at the present time that we are now paying the penalty for having Been a little too boastful of our own great country. I would be the last in the world to disparage the natural greatness of Canada, but we must take a sensible and a judicial view of these matters. We live side by side with a country upon whom a munificent Providence has seen fit to shower natural blessings which are even greater than ours. Take the climate, for instance, I admit that a man from a cold country may prefer our cold and rigorous climate, but a man from the average country of Europe prefers that of the United States, and that is one of the reasons why the early settlers chose to settle there, and from that nucleus the United States has built up a population of about one hundred and ten millions, whereas we have only the paltry number, by comparison, of eight or nine millions. They can grow corn. We have the soil for that too, but we have not the sun. Our quantity of corn is almost negligible, but we all know what an imimense natural asset that product is to the United States in an agricultural sense. They can grow cotton, an enormous natural asset to them, while we, of course, cannot grow any of that. When you come to fruit, it is true that we have some of the finest-flavoured fruit in the world, but in quantity it is small compared with the gigantic areas of fruit that are to be found in California and Florida, and we are glad to import their fruit despite the plaint the other day from the right hon. leader of the opposition. Take the rainfall. In 1918, when the hurricane of the war had reached its height, we were disposed to claim that this country was the granary of the Empire, but in that very year Providence saw fit to withhold very largely the rainfall from our prairies, and He saw fit to give the United States their rainfall, which is usually more dependable than in our great West, and it fell to the United States to help feed England whose tenacity was being tried to the utmost, and we had a very small part in that particular work for that year. Take our seaboard. We all know when we look at the map that we have a comparatively short seaboard on the Atlantic, and it is very jagged too. In winter the greater pait of it is in the grip of the ice king, but that is not so with the Atlantic seaboard
The Address-Mr. Putnam

of the United States. The great ships turn their prows for the United States as coming to a climate which is just a little bit warmer and more comfortable, and to harbours which know no ice and which average a better approach than they find on our shores, and the great freighters and the ocean greyhounds put into United States ports, and it is hard indeed to persuade their owners to give us any fair proportion, of their traffic. Now, I do not want to be misunderstood as to all this. I trust that no man, or no woman, would be cowardly enough to go out and say I was running down my country: I am simply trying, Mr. Speaker, to preach a little lesson in modesty. I think that we sometimes have run away with the idea that our country was unique in its natural resources and in its opportunities. It is not. But I do proclaim, and very broadly, that after all we have comparatively a very great country and its greatness, one of its assets, will be the raising of a virile, an intellectual, a spiritual and an imaginative people. Mr. Speaker, in so far as we have the will to win, in so far as we conquer difficulties, in so far as we overcome the obstacles of geography, the obstacles of distance-the fact that the habitable and the cultivable part of this country is largely found stretched, almost like a shoe string, along only the southern part of it-all that is an inspiration for us to put our best brain, pur best patriotism, and our best patience into working out some solution, some honourable compromise, whereby we shall make an ultimate and glorious success of Canada. It is going to take patience. The competition from the United States is such that if you spend money in bringing immigrants here, we know very well they are apt to percolate down to the United States, and the money we have spent in bringing them here goes for nothing. That is one of the objections which the armchair critics on this question of immigration do not take into account. They say "Why do you not encourage immigration as Australia did?" But the Australian continent is a great island, with a warm climate, with frost and snow almost unknown. When you get an immigrant there, it is no matter if he is dissatisfied, there is no United States border for him to slip across; he has to stay there and make the best of it. That is one of our difficulties and my point, if I may be clear is this: We should try to solve the problems of our country. It is all a fallacy and a waste of time to sit down and enumerate only the features which indicate the greatness and the advantages of our country. Let us diagnose the case. Let us look at our difficulties along

with our advantages. Let us face them candidly and frankly and let us in this investigation quit us like men. We have a great country, but we are subject to great competition from our neighbours to the south.
Mr. Speaker, I am trying at my age,-because I sometimes feel that I have ceased to be a young man,-to disabuse myself as far as I can of any prejudice and party spirit, and I am trying to look at things calmly as one judging a game from the side lines wherein he can see the mistakes and the excellencies of the players of both opposing teams. It is almost a truism that this party spirit should long ago have been abandoned; and I- am glad to say that, as far as my observation goes, it is pretty nearly at an end in this country.	I loath this intense
party spirit on which we were brought up, and point to the fact of sixty-five Progressives being here as a significant proof of the truth of what I am saying. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) turned to them the other day, and he put to the Progressives from the prairies this rhetorical poser: "Do you think all the wisdom of Canada is centred in you?"
I think that ex-soldier was playing with a double-edged sword. I think a fair implication as to the meaning of that remark was that he possibly thought that in his own mind there was more wisdom than in the minds of the whole of these dwellers upon the plains and their splendid representatives in this House. I must state in all good nature that I resented the question. I have two brothers in the West. They went out there just as strong Liberals as my hon. friend now professes to be a Conservative. Just as strong Liberal as I am. If I were out in the West I have no doubt I would see with the viewpoint of the people who dwell there and the representatives who come here from those districts. Those two brothers of mine supported the member who is now here from Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner). They are no longer Liberals, they think that party spirit is an absolutely foolish fetish and they lament having wasted so many years in the worship of it. Now they are Progressives. They belong to no party. They are dissatisfied with both the old parties.
I say that in this present state of affairs we should all try fo sink, as far as possible, this ridiculous handicap of frenzied party spirit. We can get an even wider outlook. Mr. Speaker, I lately saw the review of a book.
I forget the name of the author, but the subject of the book was The Patriotism of Humanity. That author put forward the position, and I saw it most favourably reviewed, that
The Address-Mr. Wilson
the man who to-day thinks that all the virtue is confined to his own country, and that all the undesirable elements of a nation are limited to some rival or some foreign country, is an antiquated specimen in the civilization of to-day, and I fancy that is the right way to view it. Do you imagine if our blessed Master were back on this earth that any more now than when He was here, we would appreciate Him as belonging to one country and being a partisan of that country and an enemy of every other. He and His great doctrines were intended for the whole world, and the sooner we learn to take that infinitely wide outlook the better for all concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I know that some recoil at the very word "compromise", but I remember reading a speech by Sir George Foster, who now adorns the Senate, in 1895 or 1896, when a troublous question was before this House. He said: Let us grasp and bear aloft the torch of friendly compromise under which the Fathers of Confederation marched in times far less prosperous and far more troublous than our own to an era of progress and continued peace. I think that view is peculiarly in point in presence of the problems of the present day.
In conclusion I merely wish to say that, as I judge the atmosphere at this time, at this capital city, and in this parliament, I am in hopes that the budget, which the present administration is working so hard to evolve, will be one in which the greater number, and the preponderating influence in this country will find a magnet upon which to unite in a friendly and an honourable compromise that will be to the lasting benefit of this Canada of ours.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Had it not been for the announcement of the Minister of Justice the other evening touching the extravagance of this House in regard to time, I do not think I should have stood up in my place to, in the first place, review some of the statements that have been made from both sides of the chamber, for I must
10 p.m. confess that here outside appearances do not always reflect inside experiences. But, Mr. Speaker, I can plead that perhaps in the past I have not taken up the time of this House at any too great length, and when I have spoken I trust I have been enabled to place some matters before this House, at least believing them to be true.
In the first place, I would like to congratulate and offer my felicitations to all the sons and daughters of the Emerald Isle upon the 17th of March, the day they honour their patron saint. May the land of the shamrock be favoured with prosperity and blessed with
national unity, tempered with equality and justice. I am sure that these words express the view of all those living in the Land of the Maple. I trust that any remarks I may make will be devoid of offence to all, and if I err, Sir, I hope it may not be a serious error.
I might as well say at the outset that I am of Irish and Scotch parentage, but I am a Canadian, and if, in the course of my remarks, I demonstrate some of my Scotch or Irish traits, kindly remember that one cannot refuse an inheritance, especially the Scotch. It did not cost me anything. You know an Irishman is reported to have said that every man should be proud of his native country, whether he was born there or not. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am proud that I am a Canadian and born in the county I represent, and, for your information, may I add that I am in rather a distinguished company in this House, because the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) was-born in that county; the dean of this House, the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) was born in that county, and the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) was also born in that county. It is a good county, a county where industry and agriculture work hand in hand, a little different from some of the counties I have heard from in this debate. If sentiment at any time draws me to the side of the birthplace of my parents, it is only, I hope, because I love both the shamrock and the heather, but not more than the maple leaf.
We are all delighted to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) back in his place; and may I express the hope that, during his recent visit to our cousins in the South, he has been physically benefited, nay even inoculated with that American spirit and principle of looking out for number one, and that he may transmit to his cabinet and followers in this House, and through them into the veins of public life of Canada, that serum which will result in a return to a sane policy that a Canadian government should look after Canadian interests, especially when every other country is adopting such a policy. If the Deputy Speaker had not been in the Chair, I would like to refer to the long political experience of the Speaker of this House, of some 28 years, and I would ask him if he had ever, in all the records of this House remembered such a situation as we have today. Last session we found the government in the position of practically being afraid to bring in legislation without first stating that the measure would not be considered a party measure. This session we have no sign of improvement, no signs of stability, but rather
The Address-Mr. Wilson

symptoms of a nervous break down, a complication of internal disorders that may result seriously.
I will review some of the strange situations during the Prime Minister's absence. But before doing so, may I remind the hon. Prime Minister that I read the other day that an Italian had invented a delicate instrument whereby he could tell where earthquakes were going to take place and when; and I would suggest to the hon. Prime Minister that he equip his department with one; in fact some of us may have the opinion that he already has one, and that when he heard the murmurings and rumblings in his own party he decided, perhaps, that a visit a little further South might benefit him. No doubt, Sir, what has taken place during his absence has been placed before him, but I would like to refer to it. I may refer to-what shall we call it-the anguished indecision of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler); or the position taken by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Marler), the supporter, we will say, who longs to bless, but who is constrained to curse; or the position of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) who, having heard his leader promise at Brantford that. no legitimate industry would be interfered with, and1 which upon comparing this statement with the announcement of reduction in the tariff on instruments of production, must lead him to add perhaps to1 what he has already so well said. I thought when the ex-Solicitor General, Hon. D. D. McKenzie, left the House that we had no authority left on Biblical quotations but I notice the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) is an adept at it, and I will have to be Very careful with any statements, I may make in that respect; but I would think that the attitude of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) will be found in these words-
Yea, mine own familiar friend in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
And I suppose to this the Prime Minister will no doubt reply-
They profess me with their lips but their hearts are far from me.
Then another incident took place, and I am mentioning these things in an endeavour to find out, if we possibly can, what the policy of the government is, or what their attitude to the country is. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) suddenly became converted, but his conversion will only remain permanent provided' certain things are done in his riding. Then we have the hon.

member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) who, in a statement given to the press-and strange things are happening now-comes out in favour of one of the greatest combines, mergers or trusts, that this country has ever heard of, and he announces himself at the same time in favour of the protection of the minority. I do not wish to put him in a false light, but the hon. member has come out strongly and declared himself in favour of the greatest ecclesiastical merger or trust that he can conceive; that is church union.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend says, "hear, hear". While in my public career in municipal life, when I was a member of the local legislature, and also in this House, I have never been afraid1 to face any question, and I resent very much some of the campaign literature of one of the sides of this question. If my hon. friend had not said "hear, hear", I doubt whether I would have gone into it; and especially had I not been sent a printed pamphlet in connection with one of the contesting parties in the Presbyterian church, which I attend, on this question, which pamphlet states that no doubt when this question comes up in the House politicians and members of parliament will take the line of least resistance. That has never been my attitude. I will not take the course of least resistance; but I will exercise that liberty of conscience that, I claim, is my right, and when the time comes, I will vote the way I think, in spite of petitions or letters that may be sent to me. I think I have a perfect right to hold to the views that I maintain, as part of our civil and religious liberty.
