speechtext:
It may be Scotch, but I
am proud of it. I am proud of this, that I practise what I preach. I am not like some other people that preach and do not practise.
I would also refer to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). I do not know, to be candid, what position he was in, because, while he spoke from this side and he received the greatest amount of applause from my hon. friends to my left, in the absence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) he was not making love to the then leader of the government (Mr. Graham), but he was practically what I would say skylarking with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). To-night, I saw him sitting over on that side, and I wondered if something had taken place, because while there is no doubt in my mind he is an ardent free trader, I think he is in the position

The Address-Mr. Wilson
of a prodigal son. I remember his speaking about the corn; I suppose there were corn husks where he was, and he evidently is anxious to get back. I suppose when he considers the statement made by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) about dropping the pilot, he may think there may be a change and it is pretty nearly time for him to get back.
I said that we were anxious to know what the trouble was. The other night the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) inquired of different members sitting on the government benches if they would enlighten us as to what the Speech from the Throne meant. I know there are still certain members from whom we on this side would like to hear. I should like to hear from the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Healy). You know the hon. member for North Essex says:
King needs Tim; Tim needs King;
Tim and King, that's the thing
We would like to know the position of the hon. member for North Essex on this tariff question at the present time. It would be well worth while having the opinions of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm), the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell), the gallant member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), the hon. member for Lothbiniere (Mr. Vien), and the hon. member for Chamblv and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). As regards the last three members, I can remember in previous sessions when they were sitting on this side, they were very active critics of the government; they never failed to express their opinions, and I wonder how they stand on this question to-day as presented by the government. There is another one in the ranks of the Progressive party that I would like to hear from. We have heard from the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). I would like to hear from the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Elliott). It is, however, for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) to tell what the trouble is. I have wondered, as a great many people have wondered, what the trouble was, but you know the Minister of Agriculture has that-what should I call it?-sort of perambulating "roaming in the gloaming" style of telling you, and you know just about as much after he is through as you did before he started. His statement, however, will perhaps, convince some of the members of the House and the country what the trouble is. I hope my hon. friends of the Progressive party will agree with what he thinks of it, because I think he advocates mixed farming in the West and some of them do not take kindly to that.
This is an address given by the Minister of Agriculture before the Womens Liberal Association in Ottawa, and it is taken from the Journal of 22nd January, 1924. Speaking before a women's club, this Sampson of politics had to fall for a Delilah of the Liberal Club; he had to tell wherein his strength lay or wherein the weakness lay. What does he say? The paper said in its report of his speech at this club:
It was not a prepared speech. . .
The report continued:
While believing in the two-party system of government, which he traced from the Cavaliers and Roundheads of Charles I, if people desired more than two parties they must make up their minds to have unstable government, said Mr. Motherwell. That of which he was a member was an example, carrying on without a majority, but still able to carry on. More parties invariably meant more confusion. It would probably do neither Great Britain nor Ramsay MacDonald harm to have the Labour government experiment in England. ThingS would look differently to Mr. MacDonald when he got into power.
I want to say this to my Progressive friends that if they ever happen to get into power, things will look differently to them. Further on he says:
In Canada at present politics had descended to "cut-throat euchre", with the government in the position of the dealer. It was regrettable at a time when the country needed strong legislation that the government's hands should be tied, "and that we should have to count noses before we move".

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Who said that?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture. The Assistant Clerk of this House deserved great credit when he could call the names of the members of the House; but I hope the Minister of Agriculture has no intention to introduce legislation to compel him to count noses when a vote is taken. The Minister of Agriculture has just come in. Let me repeat that I am talking about him and his wooing of the ladies of the Liberal Club of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The minister says, "hear, hear." The minister described the position of the government in saying that the game was " cut-throat euchre." It may be euchre, because as I look across at the other side of the House, the Prime Minister is not in his place, but I know that he has lost his right bower and also his left bower, and the only thing which he does now is to appeal to my hon. friends to my left and to take his partner's best, in this case the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). I want to tell him that that game is out of date. It is not according to Hoyle. You cannot take your partner's best.

The Address-Mr. Wilson

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The joker is over there.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I might ask the Minister of Agriculture if the embargo is still on, and if it is still on, what does it prevent from coming into this House or this country? The hon. member, as I stated, goes further as regards the cut-throat euchre. He said:
It was regrettable at a time, when the country needed strong legislation that the government's hands s'lou'd be tied, and that we should have to count noses before we moved. Yet the people in their wisdom placed us in that position.
Further on he says, as regards the National Railways:
Sir Henry Thornton had made good-
And then mark this:
-and so long as he continues to make good be wih have the same freedom he enjoys to-day.
So Sir Henry had better be careful, he had better "watch his step," or he will get, into difficulties, too.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with certain statements that have been made during the course of this debate. In calling attention to a prediction made by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), I would add that if his other predictions are all as far at sea as this one we do not need to pay much attention to them. He said:
The Conservative party is coming back-
Then he paused, and added:
-but with reduced numbers.
Some hon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friends applaud. Drury said that. Drury said the Conservative party was coming back with reduced numbers in the province of Ontario. If my hon. friends to the left, or my hon. friends across the floor, will count noses first, or if they will give us a chance of letting the electors of the Dominion decide, they will soon find out that the Conservative party will come-back to power with ever increased numbers.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Premature consolation is but the remembrancer of sorrow, as Goldsmith says.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the Ontario Temperance Act?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, that is going to be
put to the test pretty soon. Prohibit dancing, prohibit card playing, prohibit oleomargarine, prohibit smoking, prohibit drinking and prohibit betting, and I am sure the hon. member for Brant will not find the conditions as vastly improved as his theory would lead us to believe.
I happen to have been a follower of one of the greatest leaders that this province has ever produced. I sat in the local legislature under the late Sir James Whitney, and although, perhaps, some of the statements he made have been forgotten by many, they at least contained truth and embodied practical suggestions that have turned out to be well founded. He said on many occasions that you had to have a preponderance of public opinion behind any measure before you could enforce it. Now, somebody said something about the Ontario Temperance Act. I do not know whether he referred to me or not, but so far as that is concerned I am one of those who do not preach temperance but practise it. I have never been off the water wagon in my life, but I do not insist on forcing my views on the other fellow.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Not even
protection?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No. What I think we
should do is get together-the East and the West. In fact, there should be no East and no West. The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) says this:
There is the debt under which the farmer is labouring ; there is taxation; there is the tariff; there is transportation.
Well, I may tell my hon. friend that in Ontario the greatest part of the debt is due to the farmer administration. The debt of Ontario increased from $97,000,000 in 1919 to $243,000,000 in 1923, and this by the party that had promised economy, this by the party who said that, on the good roads policy, they were going to build roads for all the people and not certain roads for certain people. I well remember that some three years ago, I think it was, when I tried to present to this House what I thought at that time was the correct view to take in connection with the building of roads in my county, I was met with determined opposition by the then hon. leader of the Progressives, the hon. member
The Address-Mr. Wilson

for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). I did not blame him, in,a way, because I think somebody on the opposition benches at that time said we were making political capital, getting ready for an election. That may be true or it may not, but the statements I made then were not exaggerations. I pointed out that in the county which I represented, roads were being built, water-bound macadam roads, with asphalt top, at a cost of $82,000 a mile; and somebody on this side of the House, a member of the then opposition, wanted to know if those were the streets that were paved with gold. And what do you think? In a return brought down in the local legislature this year the cost was stated of the construction of the road between Toronto and Clap-pison's Comers which is in my county. I wish the Progressives could coihe and see that work. They may talk about extravagant expenditures, but they should come and see how the ex-Minister of Public Works of Ontario built roads under the Parmer administration. This road, thirty-two miles long, cost over $96,000 per mile. The hon. member says, " there is the debt under which the farmer is labouring."

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask a question? Has the party which the hon. gentleman represents discovered any political corruption in relation to those roads?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend asked the question.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me to finish? Perhaps he is equally well acquainted with the debt that burdens our Manitoba farmers at the present time, and its sources.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Increased by the present Bracken government. But in the province of Ontario we have good reason to know what the debt is.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I was not referring to any increase on the part of the Bracken government, but rather to the sources of the debt under which the farmers of Manitoba are labouring at the present time. That is what I was referring to in my speech, if I was referring to that particular phase of debt at all.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If you go into it, you find that it was a general statement-the debt under which the farmers were labouring. When I rose in this House and condemned the expenditure of money in my own constituency, 1 took an attitude which, I think, is not often enough taken in this House. I condemned the extravagance of that govem-
ment. I condemned the attitude of the exMinister of Public Works of Ontario, who sits in the seat I formerly occupied in the local legislature. I condemned it because it was extravagant. I said it was not fair for Ontario or for this government to be compelled to hand over its share of the $20,000,000 grant and give that large proportion to the county of Wentworth. I want to say to the credit of the Department of Highways that they did not approve of the roads that I condemned. The late government did not approve of them, and this government, to their credit, have not approved of them. Mr. Drury, Mr. Manning Doherty and the other satellites came into my constituency during the last Dominion election and did everything they possibly could to defeat me. They stated that I was opposed to good roads, although they knew I was not, but that I was opposed only to the extravagance of their road policy. I told the farmers of that community that although the minister was saying those roads would not cost them anything, I was satisfied that when they got the bills the story would be different. And what is the position of the county of Wentworth to-day? Twenty per cent of the cost, which we have to pay, means that the county of Wentworth has to issue debentures for $842,-
000.	That is our share, and we have to pay it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I protest against the time of this House being taken up with matters that are outside of our control. I would rather have the hon. member talk about the $300,000,000 that is left to us of fixed charges which should have been partly discharged during the war.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not
know but that I am perfectly in order. The hon. member is using the tactics that were adopted by the leader of the Progressive group when I was speaking once before. He tried to prevent me, and I was saved on that occasion by the present Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy), who was very anxious to get the facts; and I may say that if my speech was in error at that time the Liberal Association of the province of Ontario ordered 10,000 copies of it. When my hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. Warner) gets up in this House and says that I should talk about something that is connected with this House, he apparently does not know that the Department of Highways under the Dominion has something to say as regards the expenditures on roads in this country. I might retort that I have never taken up the time of this

The Address-Mr. Wilson
House in talking about the agricultural show held in my county, as he has done on many an occasion.
I would suggest this to the Department of Highways. I understand that the appropriation has been spent; I think I am correct in that as regards the province of Ontario at least, and an appeal has been made, and further appeals will no doubt be made, to this government for additional money for road building. I approve of the principle of road building, but not of the extravagant principle of road building, and I also suggest to this government that; when they draw up the next regulations in connection with the paying out of money for good roads, they take a tighter grip of it and first approve of the project before it is started. I am not casting any reflections on anyone, but I know what happened in the past in the province of Ontario, and I think it is well to offer th;s suggestion which I have done in the best interests of the country.
Now let me tell my hon. friends to my left, and the hon. member who just recently interrupted me, and who may not realize the fact, that the extravagance and non-fulfilment of their pre-election pledges led to the defeat of the Farmer government in the province of Ontario. The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) speaking in this debate a few days ago said, referring to what is promised in this clause of the Speech from the Throne: "There is transportation." I trust that the hon. member does not preach that the transportation problem will be solved by the panacea for western ills, the removal of the tariff on agricultural implements.
I also want to take exception to a statement he made in regard to residents of cities, whom he called parasites. The constituency I represent is perhaps one of the largest urban and rural constituencies in the province of Ontario. We have a great number of workers, and I do not know that it is very becoming for the hon. member to refer to them as parasites, or very becoming of him to refer to the cities as big swollen parasites that suck the life-blood of the producer. We do not look upon them in that way in the constituency from which I come, because we have there the best home market for the farmers than is to be found anywhere in the province of Ontario. I believe it is the largest market in the Dominion of Canada.
My hon. friend for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher) said, "Wheresoever the carcass is, there will the vultures be gathered together." That was the statement the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) corrected for him. Now
in the urban centre of Hamilton we can truthfully say, and this is the revised version, "Where industry thrives there are the fanners gathered together." Let me prove my point by a reference to the Hamilton market. It is a great thing to hear these Progressives and the United Farmers of Ontario say-and we heard the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) say the same thing to-night: Do away with the middleman. In the city of Hamilton market the middleman is eliminated. Yet we are told that the home market is of no value to the farmer. I have here some figures furnished me by the market clerk of the city of Hamilton. The Hamilton central market is for the sale of fresh meats, poultry, fish, butter, eggs, flowers of all kinds, fruit farm and garden produce. To that market in the city of Hamilton which is the urban centre, we have brought in each day, 9,000 gallons of milk to the two city dairies from 450 producers in the country. Yet they say the home market is of no use. Here is some further information about this home market, this Hamilton market that we are so proud of. It can accommodate 1,000 vendors of all classes in one day. I do not wish to go into all the details, but I will take just one month, that of September, 1923, and I will show you how many farmers attended that market:
Transient farmers	 4,795
Farmers reserving stands	  2,213
Butchers reserving stands	 258
Fishmongers (all citizens of	Hamilton)	
72Stalls occupied by different	dealers	in produce. 144Florists	
279
In the butter hall where the farmers' wives sell their produce there were 1,621, or a total of farmers and their wives selling on the Hamilton market in the month of September, of 9,382. Yet our friends from the West tell us that the home market is of no value to us. Let me tell them what is sold there. You know, there was a United Farmers of Ontario organization-there is not much of it left to-day-for co-operative dealing, co-operative buying and selling. We heard a lot about that, but the farmers in our county have realized that it does not pay to sell through that organization, and the farmers bring their produce into the market. In the month of September there was sold on the Hamilton market, carcasses of beef, 468; calves, 599; lambs, 700; sheep, 78; hogs, 180.
I resent, Mr. Speaker, any member referring to the residents of the cities as parasites, and I want to say this so far as my constituency is concerned:	In 1914 those so-called parasites toed the scratch. They were the men who went without conscription. They walked right in, and signed up, and fought for the protection of this country and of the British
The Address-Mr. Wilson

flag. They may be parasites, but we are proud of them. I do not mind anyone calling me names; you can call me what you like, but I do resent the people I represent being called names.
On one occasion Mr. Biggs, ex-minister of Public Works of Ontario, made the statement that "politics was the dirtiest game he ever was in." I sometimes get sick and tired of hearing people say that if they had the opportunity they would do the same as others have done for their own profit. Any game is just what you make it. If you play the game fairly you would never be able to say that politics is a dirty game. But I think if we possess our souls in patience we will find that the declaration I have just quoted will be established,-that it will prove a boomerang to the man who uttered it.
I wish to say this as regards the policy of protection. I represent a manufacturing town, the town of Dundas. I also represent a large portion of the city of Hamilton. In that portion there are more American industries than in any other city in the Dominion. To those who claim that protection has not been a good thing I want bo know how it is these American industries came to Hamilton. Was it because of free trade? No, it was because there was a tariff against their goods coming into this country, and they decided to come to Canada and to manufacture in this country. That I consider is a benefit to the Dominion. In my constituency we believe in the protection of labour, we are not in favour of creating a standard of living lower than that which exists to-day. We maintain that the artisans of Wentworth county are entitled to protection; are entitled to the fair-wage clause in public contracts; are entitled to the eight-hour day; are entitled to the Minimum Wage Act; are entitled to the Workmen's Compensation Act as it exists in Ontario; and are entitled to better their condition of living. We not only believe in a policy of protection for the working men but we believe in a policy of protection for the fruit growers and market gardeners of the Niagara peninsula. We say they also need protection, and we ask the government to grant this protection. We say to our friends in the East who declare they wish to encourage agriculture : Is it fair to ask the workers in our county, in our market gardens, who work early and late, to compete against the southern states where the climatic conditions are such that it is utterly impossible for us in this Dominion to produce fruits and vegetables at as early a season as they do. I heard the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) refer to producing pineapples under glass. {Mr. Wilson.]
That may be a debatable question-putting a tax upon oranges, bananas, pineapples and lemons.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Grapes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is a duty on grapefruit, and there is a duty on grapes. But let me ask this question:	Do hon. members
know what made the price of grapes go up in the province of Ontario?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Prohibition.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, it is due to the fact that hon. gentlemen to my left, the Progressives and their friends who pronounced in favour of prohibition, absolutely refused to interfere with native wine. They preach one thing and practise another. To-day we are in this ridiculous position in the province of Ontario: It is perfectly legal to make wine from the juice of the grape, but you must get a permit if you wish to make it out of dandelions; it is perfectly legal for a wine manufacturer to sell wine containing 20 per cent of alcohol, he can manufacture it, but if he advertises it he violates the law; we cannot have 2( per cent beer but we can have wine with a 20 per cent kick in it. I believe in temperance, I make no bones about it-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Who passed that law?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Conservative government. I am not in favour of the repeal of the Ontario Temperance Act, I am in favour of sane legislation, and I commend the Premier of Ontario for the fact h.e has backbone enough to fulfil the pledges he gave to people when he was appealing for their votes. This should be an example to my right hon. friend the Prime Mininster of Canada. The trouble to-day in our public life is that the leaders of thought in religion and in municipal, provincial and Dominion politics are not living up to the pledges they gave the people.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friends may laugh,
but they should remember that Drury laughed at one time. I ask them to remember the old saying "Empty vessels make the most noise".
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to go further and refer to the industries in the city of Hamilton as an evidence that protection is a good thing. The leader of the government the other night made a strong appeal in peroration to the Grand Old Man of Hamilton, Mr. Adam Brown. We are proud of Mr. Adam Brown in the city of Hamilton, and the Dominion should

The Address-Mr. Wilson
be equally proud that when he was in political life he was a man of vision. He was one of those who believed that Canada had a great future. Mr. Brown was a member of the House in 1887, and speaking of the protection that was being afforded to the iron industry, a protection that was opposed by the Liberal opposition, he said,-and I quote from Hansard of May 17, 1887, page 494:
Mr. Brown: Hon. gentlemen opposite say hear, hear.
I hope they will get some sense knocked into them before long that they will see this in a proper light. They do see it, Mr. Speaker. The wriggling way in which they have gone through the question to-day shows that they see it. Here and there some of them try the circus trick, riding on the backs of two horses, free trade here and National Policy somewhere else. At the same time they feel that the country is so sound on the question of the National Policy that they dare not come out openly and speak against it. This change in the tariff, I believe, will secure for the National Policy a position which it has never had before, because it strikes at the root of the whole matter. It protects the labour that is required to produce the article.
The letter was read stating-
Your telegram received; we wired you this morning: "We think changes made in the tariff will be found satisfactory and will, as intended, rapidly develop the iron business." We are surprised to know the decided stand made by the government upon the tariff, the same arguments having been offered before and no result came. We had feared that the matter would be left as before, especially as such strong protests are made by prominent parties. The action of the government in taking this firm and comprehensive stand will, before long entitle them to the praise of all who take an interest in the development of this country. Increased wealth and population are sure to follow. Every ton of the ore and coal that now lies worthless in the ground, that is manufactured, adds so much to the wealth of this country.
Has Mi. Brown's prophecy been fulfilled?
This government haa been presented with a petition on behalf of the industries of Hamilton. It was moved in the council by a Liberal controller and was seconded by a Conservative controller, and another controller a Mr. Davis, who was past president of the Liberal Association, said that this was a question that certainly interested Hamilton, and what he was in iavour of was not a reduction on agricultural implements, but that he was in favour of a return to the Laurier tariff. Now if you give the manufacturers the Laurier tariff on agricultural implements I think they will be more than satisfied, and that comes from a gentleman who was a Liberal candidate in the last provincial election. This petition is addressed to the government and is from the city council, and has been sent to the Acting Minister of Finance. It says that a reduction in the duties 26
threatens the life and existence of many other Hamilton industries. They are referring to the Libbey-Owens Glass Works, and more especially to the agricultural implement manufacturers. In the city of Hamilton we have some 72 branches of American factories, and you ought to know what is taking place by the reduction even of last year. We have what is known as the International Harvester Company,-and I cannot understand why the government would single out any one industry, and especially why should they single out practically the hospital ship of Canadian industry, and they are not even going to give it a fair burial, but they are going to torpedo it; there is no question what it means. At the present time the International Harvester Company have an investment of fifteen million dollars in Hamilton and Stratford. They pay one million dollars per year in freight rates. They have in Hamilton,-under ordinary conditions in the past, an employee list of four thousand. To-day they have four hundred and fifty. That is four hundred and fifty as against four thousand. The National Steel Car Company, with a list of fifteen hundred employees, has today twelve hundred. Why have they twelve hundred? Why is it when the other company has a great proportion of their men out of work, the National Steel Car Company seem to have a large number of men at work? The reason is that the department of the Canadian National tailways has given an order to the National Steel Car Company for a thousand cars. We have another industry which so far has not been affected,-and if the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon) were in his place, he would bear out this statement-I refer to the Canadian WTestinghouse. They ordinarily employ three thousand people. They have at the present time twenty-five hundred, and the reason they have so many is because the elec trieal industry has not been disturbed to a great extent. The Hydro-Electric development in Ontario has been a factor in keeping these men employed. But to sum up, in the past, the 72 American industries had on their payroll 17,463, and they paid out $360,000 per week. To-day they have only 7,939 on their payroll. That is a reduction in the number of 9,524, and their payroll has been reduced in these industries alone from $360,000 per week to $165,210. Now, we have in the city of Hamilton other industries, and I just want to mention this fact because when the hon. Prime Minister referred to the former member from Hamilton, Mr. Adam Brown, I want to



The Address-Mr. Wilson
know if the prediction made by that gentleman in this House has come true. In 1879 the population in Hamilton was 34,208, and the assessment was 815,168,280. In 1923 the city of Hamilton had a population of 120,235 and an assessment of 8145,000,000. There are employed in the Hamilton industries 30,454; capital invested 8142,000,000; payroll per year 840,000,000. Then we have an annual incoming railway tonnage of 750,000, we have an outgoing railway tonnage of 2,500,000 tons. We have a lake shipping, outgoing of 53,000 tens, and incoming shipping of 46,000 tons.
What is the trouble to-day in the Dominion of Canada? In the first place, a great deal of our troubles arise from unemployment. And unemployment is brought about by what? The failure of someone to provide industry, the failure of the government to bring in a stable fiscal policy and the fact, as I said before, that a great many people have lost faith in the present leader of the Liberal party. They were talking about the emigration to the States. I will give the House one instance. I am not talking in the calamity strain that I sometimes hear in this House, but I will refer to one of the employees of one of the industries in Hamilton who had been for seventeen years with the same company. He has a family of eleven children, all Canadians, seven of whom are of working age. But they cannot find employment now, so he has had to resign his position, and with his family, go to the States. You talk about the policy of immigration, but do you not think, in the first place, Mr. Speaker, that we should have something to which we could invite the immigrants to come? We do not want to be a clearing house for the United States. That is what we are to-day. We are paying for the education of the people who come here, and they drift, and drift, and drift, over to the United States. Now then, if this agricultural implement industry is torpedoed, if they are driven out of business, what will happen? I would like to know from the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and leading members of the Progressive party what is going to take place supposing we do not get the tariff reduction. We heard the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) say to-night that he would be satisfied, and the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) said that he would be satisfied, with the government. I think it would be better if they would approve the idea of practically crossing the floor of the House. They cannot any longer admit that they are an independent group, because practically every one of them has said: We will support the government provided that so and 
so is done; we will support the government if they build the Hudson Bay railway.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend says: "hear,
hear." I do not deny that perhaps the Hudson Bay railway should be built, but certainly what should be done is first to have a careful investigation whether it is going to be any good or not. I have been an advocate of public ownership; I stumped the whole province in the interest of public ownership in connection with the Hydro-Electric; but I could not follow Sir Adam Beck entirely when he advocated the system of hydro-radials that he did advocate, I voted against it in my own constituency; my constituency voted for it. I am in favour of electric raliways; I am in favour of railways being built where they are needed; but I am not in favour of a policy in Ontario as regards electric roads similar to what we have in regard to steam roads. If you go into Cobourg or any of those places on the way to Ottawa, you will see three railways within a stone's throw of one another. We should be careful of what is done and we should spend our money to the best advantage.
I have already delayed this House at too great length; I apologise if I have taken longer than I should; but I hope the government will realise that the country expects something from them. The country should have had some announcement, if not in the Speech from the Throne, then one that will set at ease capital and industry in Canada. Our problems to-day, as I said, are unemployment, stagnation of business, sectionalism, transportation and proper marketing. I think one of our solutions would be the appreciation of the industrial East of the agricultural West, and the appreciation of the agricultural West, of the industrial East. Let me conclude by saying what I believe should be-and I quote in verse-the policy of this country:
Consider well 'tis not the time to stunt our growing powers,
And place this country's destiny in other hands than ours;
So let our final answer be, and let East and West be told.
We'll weld together what we have, and what we have, we'll hold.
On motion of Mr. Graham, the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Graham the House adjourned at 11.15 p.m.
